definition.text: The carbon cycle is the exchange of carbon among living things, soils, rocks, water and the air of Earth.

facts.text: Carbon is the main ingredient of living matter and a major part of many rocks, such as limestone.
The cycle covers carbon being recycled through living things and also its long-term storage in, and release from, carbon sinks.
The steps of the carbon cycle are key to making Earth able to support life.
In the air, carbon exists mainly as carbon dioxide and methane, both of which trap heat and drive part of the greenhouse effect.
Carbon dioxide leaves the air mainly through photosynthesis, entering life on land and in the ocean.
About 500 gigatons of carbon are held above ground in plants and other organisms, while soil holds about 1,500 gigatons.
Global average atmospheric carbon dioxide reached a record 422.7 parts per million in 2024.
Antoine Lavoisier and Joseph Priestley first described the carbon cycle, and Humphry Davy popularised it.

title: Carbon pools and reservoirs

definition.text: A carbon pool, or reservoir, is a part of the Earth system, such as the air, ocean or soil, where carbon is held in some form for a period of time.

facts.text: The global carbon cycle is usually split into major carbon pools linked by pathways of exchange.
The pools include the ocean, sediments including fossil fuels, the land biosphere with its soils, the atmosphere and the rocks of the geosphere.
Most of Earth's carbon is stored inertly in the rocks of the lithosphere.
The deep ocean is the largest pool of actively cycled carbon, holding 50 times more than the atmosphere, but it exchanges carbon with the surface only over hundreds of years.
About a third of soil carbon is stored in inorganic forms such as calcium carbonate.
Pool is the broader term: a carbon sink is one particular kind of carbon pool.

distinct_from: Human impact on the carbon cycle

title: Fast and slow carbon cycles

definition.text: Carbon moves in a fast cycle through living things and a slow cycle through rocks.

facts.text: The fast, biological cycle can finish within years, carrying carbon from the air into living things and back again.
The slow, geological cycle can take millions of years, moving carbon through the crust between rocks, soil, ocean and air, and may reach deep into the mantle.
How the fast carbon cycle responds to human activity will decide many of the more immediate impacts of climate change.
Though slow, the geological part is one of the most important controls on how much carbon is in the air, and so on global temperatures.

distinct_from: Human impact on the carbon cycle

title: Deep carbon cycle
article: Carbon cycle#Processes within slow carbon cycle

definition.text: The deep carbon cycle is the slow movement of carbon between Earth's surface and its deep interior.

facts.text: Carbon mainly enters the mantle as carbonate-rich sediments on ocean plates that sink beneath other plates.
Without this return of carbon to the Earth, carbon would build up in the atmosphere to extremely high levels, so it helps keep conditions fit for life.
A 2011 study of rare super-deep diamonds from Brazil showed that carbon cycling reaches the lower mantle.

distinct_from: Human impact on the carbon cycle

title: Human impact on the carbon cycle
article: Carbon cycle#Human influence on fast carbon cycle

definition.text: Since the Industrial Revolution, human activity has greatly disturbed the carbon cycle by moving huge amounts of carbon out of the ground.

facts.text: Extracting and burning fossil fuels, which moves carbon straight from rock into the air, is the largest and one of the fastest growing human impacts.
As of 2020 about 450 gigatons of fossil carbon had been extracted, nearly as much as is held in all living land biomass.
Heating limestone to make clinker, the raw material of cement, also releases carbon dioxide.
Clearing forests for farms or cities releases carbon from land ecosystems into the air.
Land-use change has also cut biodiversity, weakening ecosystems' resilience and their ability to remove carbon from the air.
Small amounts of halocarbon gases caused about 10% of the direct radiative forcing from long-lived greenhouse gases in 2019.
For now, carbon exchanges between the air and the rest of the Earth system act as negative feedbacks that dampen the climate effect of human emissions.

definition.text: A carbon sink is a carbon pool, natural or artificial, that takes up more carbon from the atmosphere than it releases.

facts.text: Sinks are an important part of the natural carbon cycle.
Globally, the two most important carbon sinks are vegetation and the ocean.
Soils hold more carbon than all land plants and the atmosphere together, but intensive farming has severely depleted the carbon in many agricultural soils.
For gases other than CO2, a sink need not store the gas; it can break it down, as when nitrous oxide is reduced to harmless N2.
Artificial sinks store carbon in building materials or deep underground, but no major artificial system yet removes carbon from the air on a large scale.
Deforestation and industrial agriculture have depleted natural sinks, and this land-use change is one cause of climate change.
Public awareness of sinks grew after the 1997 Kyoto Protocol promoted their use as carbon offsets.

title: Forests as carbon sinks

definition.text: Forests act as carbon sinks by taking carbon dioxide from the air and storing it as wood, roots and leaves.

facts.text: Forests take up about 25% of human carbon emissions each year.
Forests can turn from carbon sinks into carbon sources.
In 2019 forests absorbed a third less carbon than in the 1990s, because of higher temperatures, droughts and deforestation.
The typical tropical forest may become a carbon source by the 2060s.
Avoiding deforestation is better than clearing and later replanting, which causes lasting biodiversity loss and soil damage.
Forests can switch from sinks to sources of carbon; in 2019 they took up a third less carbon than in the 1990s because of heat, drought and deforestation.
New forests take several decades to match the carbon benefit of keeping mature forests standing, so scientists call protecting natural forests the major climate solution.
Stored carbon only stays out of the air if trees are not burned and do not rot when they die.

contested_note: The estimate of 0.9 billion ha of extra tree canopy has been criticised as too high once albedo is counted.

title: Enhancing natural carbon sinks
article: Carbon sink#Purpose in the context of climate change

definition.text: Enhancing natural carbon sinks means managing forests, soils and other ecosystems so they remove more CO2 from the air and store it durably.

facts.text: Preserving and enhancing carbon sinks is an important climate change mitigation measure.
It requires changes in farming and forestry, such as preventing deforestation and restoring ecosystems by reforestation.
Restoring ecosystems and converting less land are among the tools that can cut the most emissions before 2030.
The 2022 IPCC report calls these land-based options AFOLU mitigation, for agriculture, forestry and other land use.
Proposed ocean methods such as seaweed farming and ocean fertilisation have not yet been used at large scale.

definition.text: Buildings made of mass timber can act as artificial carbon sinks, because the wood keeps the carbon the trees took from the air.

facts.text: Replacing steel and concrete with timber could store between 10 million and close to 700 million tons of carbon a year, depending on the scenario.
This needs sustainably managed forests and reuse or preservation of the wood when buildings are demolished.
Fast-growing plant materials such as bamboo, straw or hempcrete can add further storage.

definition.text: A biogeochemical cycle is the movement and transformation of chemical elements and compounds between living things, the air and the Earth's crust.

facts.text: The major cycles include the carbon, nitrogen and water cycles.
In each cycle a substance is changed and moved by living things and through stores such as the air, the soil and the oceans.
Energy flows one way through ecosystems, arriving as sunlight and leaving as heat, but the matter that makes up living things is conserved and recycled.
Six elements common in living matter, carbon, nitrogen, hydrogen, oxygen, phosphorus and sulfur, take many chemical forms as they cycle.
Geological processes such as weathering, erosion, drainage and plate subduction also help recycle materials, which is why the cycles are called biogeochemical.
Microorganisms drive much of the cycling of elements in the Earth system.
Climate change and other human impacts are changing the speed, intensity and balance of many of these cycles.

definition.text: A reservoir is a place where a chemical is held for a long time, and residence time is how long it stays in one place.

facts.text: Coal deposits are a reservoir that stores carbon for a long time.
Places that hold a chemical only briefly, such as plants and animals, are called exchange pools.
Reservoirs are generally non-living parts of the environment, while exchange pools are generally living things.
Residence time is also called turnover time, renewal time or exit age.

definition.text: A box model simplifies a complex system into boxes, or storage reservoirs, for a material, linked by flows of that material.

facts.text: Box models are widely used to model biogeochemical systems.
Each box is assumed to be evenly mixed, and simple models are used to derive formulas for the dynamics and steady-state amounts of a chemical.
In a one-box model, a source Q flows into the reservoir and a sink S flows out; the budget balances the two.
The reservoir is in steady state when Q equals S, so its contents do not change over time.

title: Nitrogen cycle

definition.text: The nitrogen cycle is the biogeochemical cycle in which nitrogen changes between chemical forms as it moves among the air, land and sea.

facts.text: Its main steps are fixation, ammonification, nitrification and denitrification.
Nitrogen makes up 78% of the atmosphere, but that gas is hard for living things to use, so usable nitrogen is scarce in many ecosystems.
Nitrogen availability can set the rate of key ecosystem processes such as primary production and decomposition.
Many of its steps are carried out by microbes harvesting energy or gathering nitrogen to grow.
Plants take up nitrate or ammonium from the soil through their root hairs.
Growing legumes, making fertilizer with the Haber–Bosch process and burning fuels have more than doubled the yearly conversion of nitrogen into forms life can use.

related: Human impact on the nitrogen cycle

definition.text: Ammonification, or mineralization, is the conversion by bacteria and fungi of nitrogen in dead matter and wastes into ammonia or ammonium.

facts.text: When a plant or animal dies or an animal excretes waste, its nitrogen starts in organic forms such as amino acids and DNA.
It is the last step of the nitrogen cycle that involves organic compounds.
Mineralization rises with soil organic nitrogen, soil microbial biomass and average yearly rainfall.

definition.text: Anammox, short for anaerobic ammonium oxidation, is a microbial process in which nitrite and ammonium are turned directly into nitrogen gas and water.

facts.text: It accounts for a major share of nitrogen conversion in the oceans.
The bacteria that carry it out were identified in 1999, to the great surprise of scientists.

definition.text: The marine nitrogen cycle is the movement of nitrogen through the ocean, similar overall to the land cycle but with different organisms and pathways.

facts.text: Nitrogen enters seawater through rain, runoff or as gas from the air, and must be fixed, mostly by cyanobacteria, before phytoplankton can use it.
Without new supplies of fixed nitrogen, the ocean's fixed nitrogen would be used up in about 2000 years.
Nitrogen arriving in the sunlit layer from upwelling or fixation is called new nitrogen; nitrogen recycled there from eaten or respired matter supports regenerated production.
Ocean acidification may cut nitrification and denitrification, letting fixed nitrogen build up and possibly causing eutrophication.

title: Reactive nitrogen

definition.text: Reactive nitrogen, or fixed nitrogen, is every form of nitrogen in the environment other than nitrogen gas (N2).

facts.text: Common forms include nitrogen oxides, ammonia, nitrous oxide and nitrate.
Just over half of the reactive nitrogen entering the biosphere comes from human activity such as fertilizer production.
Its generation has risen more than 10-fold in the past century with industrialisation, and it accumulates because it is made faster than denitrification removes it.
An excess can cause problems such as eutrophication.

related: Human impact on the nitrogen cycle

title: Nitrate pollution of drinking water
article: Nitrogen cycle#Impacts on human health: nitrate accumulation in drinking water

definition.text: Nitrate pollution is the build-up of nitrate from human activities in groundwater and surface water, where it can harm human health.

facts.text: Heavy use of nitrogen fertilizer in farming is a significant source of nitrate pollution.
Nitrate dissolves easily and is held poorly by soil, so it readily escapes to groundwater.
Other diffuse sources include livestock feeding, human and animal contamination, and municipal and industrial waste.

title: Phosphorus cycle

definition.text: The phosphorus cycle is the biogeochemical cycle that moves phosphorus through rocks, water and living things.

facts.text: Unlike most other cycles, the air plays almost no part, because phosphorus rarely becomes a gas.
Living things need phosphorus as part of DNA, RNA and ATP, and in animals it also strengthens bones and teeth.
Phosphates move quickly through plants and animals but very slowly through soil and ocean, making this one of the slowest biogeochemical cycles.
Its four main steps are uplift of phosphorus-bearing rock, weathering and erosion, transport by rivers to lakes and the ocean, and burial in sediments.
On land, the release of phosphorus as rocks weather limits how much is available to ecosystems.
Phosphorus can limit the growth of aquatic life, and phosphates from fertilizers, sewage and detergents can pollute lakes and streams.
Freshwater algal blooms are generally caused by excess phosphorus, while saltwater blooms tend to come from excess nitrogen.

distinct_from: Human impact on the phosphorus cycle

title: Human impact on the phosphorus cycle

definition.text: Humans have greatly changed the phosphorus cycle, mainly by mining phosphate rock for fertilizer.

facts.text: Since the 1840s about 110 teragrams of phosphorus have been added to the environment.
Global phosphorus mining rose 72-fold from 1900 to 2022, with an expected rise of 4% a year.
At this pace of mining, slow geological processes cannot replace what is lost.
Humans have raised the net storage of phosphorus in soil and ocean systems by an estimated 75%, increasing ocean eutrophication.

title: Nitrogen-to-phosphorus ratio

definition.text: The nitrogen-to-phosphorus (N:P) ratio compares the amounts of these two plant nutrients, and human activity has pushed it out of its normal balance.

facts.text: Both nutrients are widely used in farm fertilizers.
Over the last 40 years the N:P ratio has risen from 19:1 to 30:1, leaving phosphorus less available to ecosystems.
The cause is both extra nitrogen pollution and phosphorus being trapped during water treatment.
As the ratio rises, organisms find it harder to grow.

distinct_from: Human impact on the phosphorus cycle

title: Dust as a nutrient carrier

definition.text: Dust storms carry phosphorus and other nutrients in weathered rock particles over long distances.

facts.text: Large dust events can supply phosphorus to areas where its lack would otherwise limit growth.
Dust also carries potassium, calcium and magnesium, so storms matter for nutrient cycling.
Phosphorus blown from northern Africa is thought to help support the rich biodiversity of the Amazon rainforest.

distinct_from: Human impact on the phosphorus cycle

title: Wetlands for nutrient removal

definition.text: Wetlands are often used to remove excess nitrogen and phosphorus from water and so ease eutrophication.

facts.text: In wetlands nitrate is turned into nitrogen gas and released to the air, while phosphorus is held by wetland soils and taken up by plants.
Wetland soils can hold only a limited amount of phosphorus, so continued removal needs new soil built from plant and microbial debris.

distinct_from: Human impact on the phosphorus cycle

definition.text: Photosynthesis is the process by which plants, algae and cyanobacteria turn light energy, usually from the sun, into chemical energy.

facts.text: Usually it means oxygenic photosynthesis, which splits water and releases oxygen.
The captured energy is stored in carbon compounds such as sugars, starch and cellulose, which cells later break down through cellular respiration.
It produces and maintains the oxygen in Earth's air and supplies most of the energy for complex life.
Global photosynthesis captures energy at about 130 terawatts, about eight times the power used by human civilization.
Photosynthetic organisms turn around 100–115 billion tons of carbon into biomass each year.
Oxygen released by cyanobacteria oxygenated the Earth, which made complex life possible.
Charles Reid Barnes proposed the term photosynthesis in 1893.

definition.text: The light-dependent reactions are the first stage of photosynthesis, in which chlorophyll absorbs light to make the energy carriers ATP and NADPH.

facts.text: In plants they take place in the thylakoid membranes of chloroplasts.
Chlorophyll absorbs a photon and loses an electron, which travels down an electron transport chain to reduce NADP to NADPH.
Chlorophyll regains its electron when water is split, which releases oxygen.

definition.text: The Calvin cycle is the light-independent stage of photosynthesis, in which the enzyme RuBisCO captures CO2 from the air and builds it into sugars.

facts.text: It uses the ATP and NADPH made by the light-dependent reactions to form carbohydrates such as glucose.
Its simple sugars become cellulose, building blocks for fats and proteins, or fuel for respiration.
Melvin Calvin and colleagues worked out the pathway at Berkeley in the late 1940s, and Calvin won the 1961 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

definition.text: Carbon concentrating mechanisms are ways some plants and algae raise the CO2 level around RuBisCO so photosynthesis keeps working.

facts.text: In hot, dry weather plants close their stomata to save water, so CO2 falls and wasteful photorespiration rises.
C4 plants first fix CO2 into a four-carbon acid using the enzyme PEP carboxylase.
C4 and CAM plants avoid photorespiration this way, raising photosynthesis yield in some high-energy environments.
Cyanobacteria concentrate CO2 inside structures called carboxysomes.

definition.text: Photosynthetic efficiency is the share of light energy a plant turns into chemical energy, usually 3–6%.

facts.text: It varies with light colour and intensity, temperature and CO2 level, from 0.1% to 8%.
Mass-produced solar panels convert light to electricity at about 6–20%, and over 40% in laboratory devices.
Scientists study photosynthesis hoping to breed plants with higher yields.

definition.text: Total photosynthesis is limited by environmental factors: light, leaf area, CO2 supply, water and temperature.

facts.text: Shading by other plants is a major limit on photosynthesis.
As CO2 concentrations rise, sugar production rises until some other factor limits it.
RuBisCO binds both CO2 and oxygen, fixing CO2 when CO2 concentration is high.

title: Water cycle

definition.text: The water cycle, or hydrologic cycle, is the continuous movement of water, changing between liquid, ice and vapour, on, above and below the Earth's surface.

facts.text: The total mass of water on Earth stays fairly constant, but how it is split between ice, fresh water, salt water and air varies with climate.
Water moves by evaporation, transpiration, condensation, precipitation, sublimation, infiltration, surface runoff and subsurface flow.
The cycle is powered by energy from the sun.
The ocean is the source of 86% of global evaporation.
Most rain falls back into the ocean or onto land, where it flows over the ground as surface runoff.
Moving water carries almost all eroded sediment and phosphorus from land to waterbodies, and with groundwater it carries nitrogen too.
The cycle is essential to life and plays a large role in the global climate and ocean circulation.

conflicts.text: The oceans supply about 90% of the evaporated water that enters the water cycle.
conflicts.note: Another sentence on the same page gives 86% of global evaporation.

distinct_from: Land use effects on the water cycle

title: Water storage and residence times

definition.text: A water reservoir's residence time is the average time a water molecule spends in it, a measure of the water's average age.

facts.text: Of the world's 1,386,000,000 km3 of water, about 1,338,000,000 km3, or about 97%, is in the oceans.
Ice caps, glaciers and permanent snow hold 1.7% of all water but 68.7% of all fresh water.
Average residence times range from 1 to 2 months for soil moisture to 100 to 200 years for shallow groundwater and 10,000 years for deep groundwater.
Much more water sits in storage for long periods than is moving through the cycle at any time.

distinct_from: Land use effects on the water cycle

title: Land use effects on the water cycle
article: Water cycle#Land cover and land use changes

definition.text: Changes in land use and land cover, such as cities, farm expansion and deforestation, alter the water cycle locally and regionally.

facts.text: Such changes affect rainfall, evaporation, flooding, groundwater and how much fresh water is available.
Compacted soils and paved surfaces reduce how much water soaks in and increase surface runoff.
Deforestation locally reduces soil moisture, evaporation, rain and snow, and regionally can shift temperatures and rainfall patterns.
Dams can change natural flows, lower water quality and destroy habitat for aquatic species.
Trees help regulate the water cycle, reduce soil erosion and prevent runoff, so afforestation can improve water management.

title: Water cycle intensification
article: Water cycle#Water cycle intensification due to climate change

definition.text: Water cycle intensification is the strengthening of the water cycle caused by human-driven climate change, seen since at least 1980.

facts.text: Human-caused climate change has visibly changed the global water cycle since the mid-20th century.
A warmer atmosphere can hold more water vapour, which changes evaporation and rainfall.
One result is that heavy rain events become even stronger.
It harms the availability of fresh water and affects oceans, ice sheets, the atmosphere and soil moisture.
The IPCC's 2021 Sixth Assessment Report predicted these changes will keep growing globally and regionally.

distinct_from: Land use effects on the water cycle

title: Discovery of the water cycle
article: Water cycle#Discovery of the correct theory

definition.text: The modern theory of the water cycle, that rainfall alone keeps rivers flowing, was first published by Bernard Palissy in 1580.

facts.text: In ancient times many believed the land floated on water and that river water came from under the earth.
By roughly 500 BCE Greek scholars were suggesting that much river water comes from rain.
Palissy's idea was first tested scientifically in 1674 in a study usually credited to Pierre Perrault, but was not mainstream until the early nineteenth century.

distinct_from: Land use effects on the water cycle

definition.text: Atmospheric methane is the methane in Earth's air, a powerful greenhouse gas whose rising level is causing climate change.

facts.text: Since about 1750, methane in the air has risen by about 160%, almost entirely because of human activities.
By 2025 its concentration had risen from 722 ppb before industry to 1936 ppb, the highest in at least 800,000 years.
Since 1750 methane has made up 3% of greenhouse gas emissions by mass but about 23% of climate forcing.
Its global warming potential is about 84 times that of CO2 over 20 years and 28 times over 100 years, because it is less persistent.
It is the second largest contributor to human-caused climate forcing.
Wetlands are the largest natural source, providing roughly 20–30% of atmospheric methane.
From 2010 to 2019, methane emissions caused 0.5 °C, about 30%, of observed global warming.
Cutting methane by the end of the century could make a substantial difference to meeting the Paris climate targets.

conflicts.text: Methane's warming potential is given as 34 times CO2's over 100 years and 86 times over 20 years.
conflicts.note: Other sentences on the page give 84 (20-year) and 28 (100-year); the figures may come from different assessment versions.

conflicts.text: NOAA measurements show methane build-up has nearly tripled since 1750.
conflicts.note: Other sentences give a rise of about 160% (a factor of 2.6).

title: Methane sinks
article: Atmospheric methane#Natural sinks or removal of atmospheric methane

definition.text: Methane sinks are the processes, mainly chemical breakdown in the atmosphere, that destroy or remove methane from the air.

facts.text: Breakdown as methane rises through the atmosphere is the most effective sink, removing 90% of atmospheric methane.
Soil bacteria called methanotrophs are another major sink, using methane for energy and producing CO2 and water.
Forest soils are good methane sinks, but wetland soils with high water tables are often sources instead.
An average methane molecule stays in the air about 9.6 years, but an emission affects the atmosphere for about twelve years.

definition.text: Atmospheric methane removal is a set of approaches under research to speed up the breakdown of methane already in the air.

facts.text: Because methane is a stronger greenhouse gas, removing a smaller amount of it than of CO2 would have a similar climate effect.
Methane's low background level, about 1.92 ppm against about 420 ppm for CO2, makes it harder to capture.

title: Biological pump

definition.text: The biological pump is the ocean's living process of moving carbon from the air and land runoff into the deep ocean and seafloor sediments.

facts.text: It starts with phytoplankton in the sunlit surface layer building organic and inorganic carbon compounds.
Marine phytoplankton perform half of all photosynthesis on Earth.
Uneaten phytoplankton clump together and, with zooplankton faecal pellets, sink quickly out of the surface mixed layer.
The pump moves about 11 billion tonnes of carbon into the ocean interior each year.
Without it, atmospheric CO2 would be about 400 ppm higher than today.
Warming and stratifying of the surface ocean may cut nutrient supply and primary production, weakening the pump.
Whales and seals boost surface productivity by releasing nitrogen-rich fecal plumes, a role larger before industrial fishing cut their numbers.

distinct_from: Vertical migration and the lipid pump

title: Carbonate pump

definition.text: The carbonate pump, the 'hard tissue' part of the biological pump, moves carbon to depth as calcium carbonate shells made by surface organisms.

facts.text: Organisms such as coccolithophores, foraminifera and molluscs build protective shells of calcium carbonate.
It is one of three pumps, with the solubility and biological pumps, that carry atmospheric CO2 into the ocean interior.
Ocean acidification may weaken this pump, and since carbonate helps sinking organic matter sink, the soft-tissue pump too.

distinct_from: Vertical migration and the lipid pump

title: Continental shelf pump

definition.text: The continental shelf pump is a proposed mechanism that carries carbon from shallow shelf waters into the neighbouring deep ocean.

facts.text: It is thought to occur where the solubility pump meets cool, dense shelf-floor water that flows down the continental slope.
Shallow shelf water can cool more than open-ocean water because the shallowness limits convection.

distinct_from: Vertical migration and the lipid pump

title: Marine snow

definition.text: Marine snow is the shower of dead and dying organisms, faecal matter and mineral particles that sinks from the upper ocean to the deep.

facts.text: The deep ocean gets most of its nutrients from marine snow sinking from above.
Forming and sinking aggregates of this material drive the biological pump by exporting organic matter to the deep ocean and sediments.
Many deep-sea organisms survive by feeding on marine snow.
Sinking organic matter falls at approximately 100 meters per day, and only about 1 to 3% of surface production reaches the seabed.

distinct_from: Vertical migration and the lipid pump

title: Microbial loop

definition.text: The microbial loop is a pathway in which dissolved organic carbon in the sea is taken up by bacteria and returned to the food chain.

facts.text: The term was coined by Farooq Azam, Tom Fenchel and others in 1983 to cover bacteria's role in marine carbon and nutrient cycles.
Dissolved organic carbon comes from bursting bacteria, leakage from phytoplankton, sloppy feeding by zooplankton and animal wastes.

distinct_from: Vertical migration and the lipid pump

title: Viral shunt

definition.text: The viral shunt is the recycling, by marine viruses, of microbial particles into dissolved organic matter that microbes can readily take up again.

facts.text: As much as 25% of phytoplankton primary production may be recycled within the microbial loop through viral shunting.
Viruses contribute on average 8.6% to Earth's ecosystem carbon cycle: 1.4% in the sea, 6.7% on land and 17.8% in fresh water.

distinct_from: Vertical migration and the lipid pump

title: Vertical migration and the lipid pump

definition.text: Animals such as krill, salps and fish that feed near the surface at night and go deep by day actively carry carbon to depth.

facts.text: Without vertical migration the biological pump would be far less efficient.
The lipid pump moves carbon to deeper waters in the fat reserves of zooplankton that migrate down to overwinter.

title: Remineralisation

definition.text: Remineralisation is the breakdown of organic matter into its simplest inorganic forms.

facts.text: It frees the energy stored in organic molecules and recycles matter as nutrients for other organisms.
How much sinking matter escapes remineralisation varies from place to place.

distinct_from: Vertical migration and the lipid pump

definition.text: Cellular respiration is the process by which cells break down food molecules, usually with oxygen, to make ATP, the energy carrier cells use.

facts.text: Respiration with oxygen is aerobic; respiration using another electron acceptor is anaerobic.
It is technically a combustion reaction, but one that releases energy slowly and under control.
Aerobic respiration consumes glucose and oxygen and produces carbon dioxide, water and energy.
Current estimates put the yield at around 29 to 30 ATP per glucose, below the textbook figure of 38.
Aerobic metabolism is up to 15 times more efficient than anaerobic metabolism.
Although plants take in CO2 overall, plant respiration produces about half of the CO2 released each year by land ecosystems.
The energy left after respiration is what ecologists call net primary production.

conflicts.text: The total yield from fully oxidizing one glucose molecule is 30 or 32 ATP.
conflicts.note: The same page elsewhere gives current estimates of around 29 to 30 ATP per glucose.

definition.text: Anaerobic respiration is respiration by bacteria or archaea that use an inorganic substance such as sulfate, nitrate or sulfur, rather than oxygen, to accept electrons.

facts.text: Such organisms live in places such as hydrothermal vents, digestive tracts and oxygen-free wetland soils and sediments.
Fermentation, which passes electrons to organic molecules, is also anaerobic but is not respiration.

definition.text: Dead zones are low-oxygen (hypoxic) areas in the world's oceans and large lakes where most aquatic life cannot survive.

facts.text: Hypoxia sets in when dissolved oxygen falls to 2 mg per litre or less, and mass die-offs follow below 0.5 mg per litre.
They are often caused by eutrophication: extra nitrogen and phosphorus fuel algal blooms whose decay uses up the oxygen.
A 2008 study counted 405 dead zones worldwide.
They may be permanent, temporary (lasting hours or days) or seasonal, usually in summer and autumn.
Marine dead zones were first noted in the 1970s in heavily used waters such as Chesapeake Bay, the Baltic Sea and the Black Sea.
Fertilizer runoff from the Mississippi basin causes a summer dead zone in the Gulf of Mexico that reached over 22,000 square kilometres in 2017.
Because warmer water holds less oxygen, ocean oxygen is falling and dead zones are expanding with climate change.
Recovery depends on how long and how severe the low oxygen was; brief, mild events allow fast recolonisation.

title: Economic effects of dead zones

definition.text: Dead zones harm fisheries and other sea-based businesses to a degree that depends on how long they last and where they occur.

facts.text: They cut biodiversity and bottom-dwelling populations, though extra nutrients can briefly raise catches of some species such as anchovies.
Studies estimate that gains in surrounding waters do not offset the net loss of productivity in the dead zone.
The Gulf of Mexico dead zone is reported to cost US seafood and tourism industries about $82 million a year.
Scientists do not all agree: some argue nutrient loading has enhanced some Gulf fisheries, such as red snapper.

contested_note: Scientists disagree on whether nutrient loading on balance harms or enhances some Gulf of Mexico fisheries.

definition.text: Eutrophication is the build-up of nutrients in a body of water, causing extra growth of algae and plants that can use up the water's oxygen.

facts.text: It is caused by too much of a nutrient, most often phosphates and nitrates.
It can happen naturally or be caused by sewage, industrial wastewater, fertilizer runoff and other human sources.
The resulting algal blooms and bacterial growth deplete dissolved oxygen and cause serious environmental damage.
Effects include more phytoplankton, oxygen loss, more fish kills and the loss of desirable fish species.
Surveys found 54% of lakes in Asia, 53% in Europe, 48% in North America, 41% in South America and 28% in Africa are eutrophic.
The World Resources Institute has identified 375 hypoxic coastal zones worldwide.
The word comes from the Greek eutrophos, meaning well-nourished.

definition.text: Cultural eutrophication is eutrophication caused by human activity.

facts.text: It became more visible after chemical fertilizers spread through farming in the mid-1900s green revolution.
Phosphorus and nitrogen are its two main causes, letting algae grow fast and bloom densely.
Phosphate detergents fed it until they were phased out in the 1970s; since then sewage and agriculture are the main phosphate sources.
Nitrogen pollution comes mainly from farm runoff of fertilizer and animal waste, sewage, and nitrogen deposited from the air.

definition.text: Natural eutrophication is the slow enrichment of waters by the gradual build-up of sediment and nutrients.

facts.text: It usually comes from dissolved phosphate minerals and dead plant matter collecting in water.
Lakes naturally grow more productive as they age.
Climate, geology and other outside influences also regulate the natural productivity of lakes.

definition.text: Harmful algal blooms are dense growths of algae, often caused by eutrophication, that are toxic to plants and animals.

facts.text: When the algae die or are eaten they release nerve and liver toxins that can kill animals and may threaten humans.
Algal toxins can reach people through shellfish poisoning.
Freshwater blooms are commonly nitrogen-fixing cyanobacteria, favoured when nitrogen runs short but phosphorus inputs remain high.

definition.text: Eutrophication and harmful algal blooms impose economic costs through dearer water treatment, lost fishing and shellfish harvests, and lower tourism income.

facts.text: Murkier water raises water treatment costs, and colour and smell problems arise in drinking water treatment.
Tourism suffers because the water looks less attractive and is less safe due to bacteria from decomposition.
Controlled eutrophication could in principle raise fishery output and community income, but it is not currently recommended because damage can set in quickly.

definition.text: Eutrophication harms human health mainly through excess nitrate in drinking water and exposure to toxic algae.

facts.text: Nitrates in drinking water can cause blue baby syndrome in infants and form disinfection by-products during water treatment.
Swimming in or drinking water with toxic algae can cause rashes, stomach or liver illness, and breathing or nerve problems.

definition.text: Coastal eutrophication is nutrient enrichment of coastal seas, where nitrogen is usually the main culprit.

facts.text: Nitrogen is usually the limiting nutrient in coastal waters, while phosphorus often is in fresh water.
So nitrogen levels matter more than phosphorus for controlling eutrophication in salt water.
The pressure varies with land activities in each catchment and with how well the coastal setting dilutes nutrients and exchanges oxygen.
Over the last century, rivers' yearly delivery to the oceans rose from 19 to 37 megatonnes of nitrogen and from 2 to 4 megatonnes of phosphorus.

definition.text: Eutrophication is prevented mainly by cutting nutrient pollution from sewage and from farming.

facts.text: Sewage treatment plants can be upgraded for biological nutrient removal so they discharge much less nitrogen and phosphorus.
Even good secondary treatment leaves substantial nitrogen in most sewage effluent.
Farmers are advised to apply fertilizer in the right amount, at the right time, with the right method and placement.
UN Sustainable Development Goal 14 targets a significant cut in marine nutrient pollution from land by 2025.

definition.text: Nutrient bioextraction is farming and harvesting shellfish and seaweed to remove nitrogen and other nutrients from natural waters.

facts.text: Several studies show oysters and mussels can greatly lower nitrogen levels in estuaries.
Nitrogen removal by oyster reefs could benefit polluters facing nitrogen limits, much like other nutrient trading schemes.
If oysters keep nitrogen below legal thresholds, they spare polluters the compliance costs they would otherwise face.
Seaweeds such as kelp absorb phosphorus and nitrogen, helping clean polluted waters.

definition.text: Reversing eutrophication starts with reducing nutrient inputs, though recovery can be slow.

facts.text: Recovery can take a long time, mainly because nutrients stored in sediments keep being released.
Restoration may need more than cutting inputs, because a water body can have several stable but very different states.
Phosphate-binding materials such as alum can be added to lakes to lock up phosphorus.
Finnish phosphorus removal from the mid-1970s reached 90% removal efficiency.

definition.text: Evapotranspiration is the combined movement of water into the air from open water, ice, bare soil and plants, through evaporation and transpiration.

facts.text: Evaporation moves water straight into the air from soil and water bodies, while transpiration moves water from roots through a plant and out of its stomata as vapour.
Globally, between three-fifths and three-quarters of rain and snow falling on land returns to the air this way.
It is measured in millimetres of water over a set time.
Its level depends mainly on how much water is available, how much energy is in the air and soil, and how much moisture the air can take up.
Global warming has increased evapotranspiration over land, one of the effects of climate change on the water cycle.
Measuring it is key to water resource management and irrigation planning.

title: Vegetation and evapotranspiration

definition.text: The type and density of vegetation strongly shape evapotranspiration and so how much water a landscape yields.

facts.text: Dense vegetation such as forest may raise evapotranspiration and reduce water yield.
Rainforests are an exception: they raise humidity, cool the ground and slow winds, increasing stream flows and groundwater while they stand.
Clearing rainforests often leads to desertification as soils dry out and erode.
Deforestation lowers evapotranspiration and so atmospheric moisture, which can reduce rain downwind.

related: Land use effects on the water cycle

definition.text: Potential evapotranspiration is the amount of water a crop, soil or ecosystem would evaporate and transpire if enough water were available.

facts.text: It measures the air's demand for moisture, while actual evapotranspiration also depends on how much water the surface can supply.
Actual evapotranspiration can never exceed the potential, but can fall below it when water is short.
A dryland is a place where yearly potential evaporation exceeds yearly precipitation.
It is higher in summer, on clear and windy days, and nearer the equator.

definition.text: Because water vapour flow is hard to measure directly, evapotranspiration is usually estimated indirectly.

facts.text: A catchment water balance relates the change in stored water to precipitation, evapotranspiration, streamflow and groundwater recharge, so ET can be solved for.
Energy balance methods, including the satellite-based SEBAL and METRIC algorithms, map ET pixel by pixel.
The Penman–Monteith equation, recommended by the FAO, calculates reference ET from weather data.
Weighing lysimeters measure it directly but only over small areas.

title: Haber process

definition.text: The Haber process, or Haber–Bosch process, is the main industrial method of making ammonia from nitrogen in the air and hydrogen.

facts.text: It combines the two gases over an iron catalyst, and most of the ammonia goes into nitrogen fertilizer.
Fritz Haber showed it working in the laboratory in 1909, and Carl Bosch scaled it up for BASF.
It met rising demand for fertilizer when mined niter and guano were thought too scarce for future needs.
The hydrogen usually comes from natural gas by steam reforming, which made 72% of global ammonia as of 2012.
Ammonia production uses 1–2% of global energy, causes 3% of global carbon emissions and uses 3% to 5% of natural gas.
As of 2018 it produced 230 million tonnes of ammonia a year.

related: Human impact on the nitrogen cycle
distinct_from: Economic and environmental effects of the Haber process

title: Economic and environmental effects of the Haber process

definition.text: Synthetic fertilizer from the Haber process greatly raised farm productivity and population, at the cost of energy use and nitrogen pollution.

facts.text: Vaclav Smil estimated that at 1900 yields, the 2000 harvest would have needed nearly four times more land.
Called the detonator of the population explosion, it helped world population grow from 1.6 billion in 1900 to 7.7 billion by 2018.
Nearly 50% of the nitrogen in human tissues came from the process.
Without it, modern agriculture could not support 8 billion people.
It is one of the largest sources of reactive nitrogen build-up; because crops use less than 50% of applied nitrogen, runoff harms habitats.
Making and using nitrogen fertilizer causes around 5% of all global greenhouse gas emissions.
Cheap synthetic fertilizer weakens farmers' incentive to rotate in nitrogen-fixing legumes.
Haber-process fertilizer is a typical high-carbon import that a carbon tariff might cover.

title: Human impact on the nitrogen cycle
article: Human impact on the nitrogen cycle

definition.text: Human activity, mainly synthetic fertilizer and fossil fuel burning, now adds more reactive nitrogen to the environment than natural nitrogen fixation does.

facts.text: These inputs have greatly altered the global nitrogen cycle over the past century, increasing nitrogen deposition and disrupting natural processes.
Humans have more than doubled the yearly conversion of nitrogen into biologically available forms.
Atmospheric nitrous oxide rose from about 270 nmol/mol before industry to about 319 nmol/mol in 2005; it is both a greenhouse gas and ozone-depleting.
Human activities cause 35% of global nitrous oxide emissions, about 20% from farming sources such as fertilizer and manure.
Nitrous oxide is the third largest contributor to global warming and, mass for mass, nearly 300 times more potent than CO2.
High-temperature combustion has raised the flow of nitrogen oxides to the air 6- or 7-fold, contributing to smog and acid rain.
As of 2020 the top emitters of human nitrous oxide were China (16.7%), India (10.9%), the United States (5.7%), Brazil (5.3%) and Russia (4.6%).

title: Nitrogen deposition
article: Human impact on the nitrogen cycle#Biosphere

definition.text: Nitrogen deposition is the fall of reactive nitrogen from the air onto land and water, in rain, as gases or as fine particles.

facts.text: From 1600 to 1990, deposition of reactive nitrogen to land and sea rose over 200%.
Extra deposition can acidify soils, streams and lakes and change forest and grassland productivity.
In grasslands, productivity first rises and then falls once critical thresholds are exceeded.
Nitrogen enrichment favours fast-growing species and lowers species richness, as when grasses replace species-rich heathland.

prerequisites: Human impact on the nitrogen cycle
distinct_from: Human impact on the nitrogen cycle

title: Nitrogen cascade
article: Human impact on the nitrogen cycle#Integration

definition.text: The nitrogen cascade is the passing of the same reactive nitrogen from one ecosystem to the next, through air, water and land, until it is turned back into nitrogen gas.

facts.text: Nitrogen problems are linked by pathways that carry nutrients across system boundaries.
Some systems store reactive nitrogen along the way, delaying the cascade and intensifying local effects.
Human-added nitrogen is ultimately either stored or denitrified, but their relative importance is still poorly known.
Some scientists think the cascade may be as big a problem for Earth's ecology as carbon dioxide.

related: Human impact on the nitrogen cycle
distinct_from: Human impact on the nitrogen cycle

definition.text: Environmental hypoxia means low-oxygen conditions, usually in the air at altitude or in natural waters.

facts.text: Water with 1 to 30% of its possible oxygen saturation is called hypoxic, and water with none is called anoxic.
Most fish cannot live below 30% saturation, while a healthy water body should seldom fall below 80%.
It is most often caused by nutrient pollution: algal blooms die, sink and are decomposed by bacteria that use up the oxygen.
It can also occur without pollution, as when lighter river water layers over seawater in estuaries and blocks oxygen from reaching the bottom.
Hypoxia harms air-breathing organisms but is essential for many anaerobic ones.

definition.text: Seasonal fish kills are mass deaths of fish when oxygen in a lake's deep water is used up in summer or winter.

facts.text: In summer, layering of the lake and extra organic matter speed respiration in the deep water.
In winter, ice and snow cut light for photosynthesis and block oxygen exchange with the air while respiration continues.

definition.text: Infiltration is the movement of water from the ground surface down into the soil.

facts.text: The infiltration capacity is the fastest rate at which water can soak in; it is usually measured in meters per day.
When rain falls faster than the soil can take it in, the extra water usually runs off over the surface.
Soils with small pores, such as clay, take in water more slowly than soils with large pores, such as sand; compaction lowers infiltration further.
Wet soil soaks up water more slowly; fully saturated soil cannot take in any more.
Plant roots and burrowing animals open cracks in the soil that speed infiltration; bare ground can have very low rates, causing runoff and erosion.
Pavement and other impermeable surfaces stop infiltration entirely and increase runoff.
Steeper slopes shed water as runoff more readily, lowering infiltration.

definition.text: Infiltration calculation methods are equations that estimate how much water, and how fast, soaks into soil, as one term in a watershed's water budget.

facts.text: The rigorous standard is Richards' equation, a strongly nonlinear partial differential equation that is costly to compute and not guaranteed to converge.
The Green-Ampt method depends on soil suction head, porosity, hydraulic conductivity and time.
Horton's equation is empirical: infiltration starts at an initial rate and falls exponentially to a steady rate once the soil is saturated.
The Kostiakov equation lets the intake rate decline as a power function; a modified version adds a steady intake term.

title: Mycorrhizal fungi and soil carbon
article: Mycorrhizal fungi and soil carbon storage

definition.text: Mycorrhizal fungi, which live in partnership with the roots of almost all plants, may help decide how much carbon soils store.

facts.text: Soil holds more carbon than plants and the atmosphere together.
Plants are estimated to send 5 to 20% of the carbon they take up to mycorrhizal fungi.
On forested islands in Sweden, mycorrhizal fungi held 50 to 70 percent of the carbon stored in leaf litter and soil.
Ectomycorrhizal fungi can compete with free-living decomposers for nutrients, slowing decomposition and raising soil carbon storage.

contested_note: Studies disagree on whether arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi and their protein glomalin increase soil carbon or cause net losses of it.

title: Priming effect
article: Mycorrhizal fungi and soil carbon storage#Stimulation of decomposition (priming)

definition.text: Priming is when fungi or roots release easy-to-use energy compounds that spur free-living decomposers to break down more soil carbon.

facts.text: Lab experiments found that arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi increase soil carbon losses, more so under elevated CO2.
Evidence for priming by ectomycorrhizal fungi is so far inconclusive.

definition.text: Net ecosystem production is gross primary production minus all the respiration in an ecosystem, by plants, animals and microbes.

facts.text: It is the carbon in an ecosystem that can be stored, exported, or turned back into carbon dioxide.
It is given as mass of carbon per area per time, such as grams of carbon per square meter per year.
This carbon may end up burned or broken down by sunlight, stored as biomass, exported to another system, or buried in sediments or soils.
Net primary production differs: it subtracts only the plants' own respiration, not that of animals and microbes.
Net ecosystem production is one of the main factors directly linked to methane emissions from wetlands.

definition.text: Net community production is net primary production minus the respiration of animals and other heterotrophs.

facts.text: It equals net ecosystem production; only the calculation differs.
In the tropical South Pacific annual net community production can be close to zero, while elsewhere in the Pacific it ranges from 2.0 to 2.4 mol C m−2 yr−1.

definition.text: Legumes such as clover, soybean, alfalfa and peanut house rhizobia bacteria in root nodules that make nitrogen compounds for the plant.

facts.text: When a legume dies its fixed nitrogen is released to other plants, fertilizing the soil.
Many traditional farming systems rotate fields through crops that include one mainly of clover.
Agroforestry can use nitrogen-fixing plants such as legumes to restore soil nitrogen fertility.

definition.text: Lightning fixes nitrogen by supplying enough energy to break nitrogen gas apart so it reacts with oxygen to form nitrogen oxides.

facts.text: The nitrogen oxides form nitrogen dioxide and then nitrous or nitric acid in water; in soil these yield nitrate that plants can use.
Industrial fixation with electric arcs, first described by Henry Cavendish in 1784, closely resembles fixation by lightning.

definition.text: Nutrient pollution is water pollution caused by too many nutrients, usually nitrogen or phosphorus, entering water.

facts.text: It is a main cause of eutrophication in lakes, rivers and coastal waters, where excess nutrients feed algal growth.
Sources include runoff from farms, septic tank waste, feedlots, raw sewage and emissions from burning fuels.
Nitrogen and phosphorus from fertilizer that crops do not use are lost from fields and harm air and downstream water.
Excess nitrogen causes harmful algal blooms, hypoxia, acid rain, nitrogen saturation in forests and climate change.
Its economic costs include higher water treatment costs, losses to commercial and recreational fishing and shellfish, and reduced tourism income.
Health effects include excess nitrate in drinking water (blue baby syndrome) and rashes or breathing problems from swimming in algal blooms.
Remedies include vegetated buffer zones, artificial wetlands, vegetated drainage ditches, better wastewater treatment and permits under the polluter pays principle.
In Europe agriculture is usually the main source of nitrogen in water, while households and industry often dominate phosphorus.

definition.text: Nutrient trading is a form of water quality trading, a market-based policy tool in which sources swap credits for cutting nutrient pollution.

facts.text: It rests on the fact that different polluters in a watershed can face very different costs to control the same pollutant.
Sources that can cut pollution cheaply sell reduction credits voluntarily to sources for which control is expensive.
Its underlying principle is that the polluter pays, usually backed by a rule requiring participation.
A 2013 Forest Trends report found three kinds of funders: beneficiaries of watershed protection, polluters offsetting their impacts, and public good payers such as governments and NGOs.
As of 2013, payments were overwhelmingly started by public good payers like governments and NGOs.

definition.text: Nutrient source apportionment estimates how much of the nutrient load reaching a water body comes from each sector, after treatment or natural losses.

facts.text: Load-oriented approaches work back from in-stream monitoring data; source-oriented approaches model emissions from export coefficients of similar catchments.
By identifying the sources, these models support proportional and practical management of polluted waters.

title: Ocean acidification

definition.text: Ocean acidification is the ongoing fall in the pH of Earth's ocean as it absorbs carbon dioxide from the air.

facts.text: Carbon dioxide from human activities is the main cause; dissolved CO2 forms carbonic acid, which releases hydrogen ions that lower pH.
Between 1950 and 2020 average ocean surface pH fell from about 8.15 to 8.05, roughly a 26% rise in hydrogen ion concentration.
Seawater is still alkaline, with a pH above 8; acidification means it is becoming less so.
Mollusks, corals and other organisms that build shells and skeletons from calcium carbonate are especially vulnerable.
Today's rate of change is far faster than in the geological past, too fast for organisms to adapt gradually.
Acidification occurred before, during several mass extinctions including the end-Permian and Cretaceous–Paleogene events.
Acidification combined with ocean warming harms marine life far more than either alone.
Cutting carbon dioxide emissions is the only response that addresses the root cause; carbon dioxide removal would also help reverse it.

notes: The lead (S:a2ede8cb1ab7) gives the 8.15-to-8.05 fall for 1950-2026, the body (S:afb1d50b0c37) for 1950-2020; the facts use the body's dated version.

definition.text: The saturation state (Ω) of seawater measures how readily a mineral such as calcium carbonate will form or dissolve in it.

facts.text: Ω is the product of the calcium and carbonate ion concentrations divided by the solubility product at equilibrium.
Rising dissolved CO2 lowers carbonate ion availability and so the saturation state, making shells harder to build.
Calcium carbonate is supersaturated in most surface waters and undersaturated at depth, so shells tend to dissolve as they sink; the boundary is the saturation horizon.

title: Economic impacts of ocean acidification
article: Ocean acidification#Impacts on the economy and societies

definition.text: Ocean acidification threatens commercial fisheries, shellfish harvests and coastal tourism that many people depend on.

facts.text: Future acidification may affect the livelihoods of some 470 to 870 million of the world's poorest people, depending on the emissions scenario.
About one billion people depend wholly or partly on the fishing, tourism and coastal protection services of coral reefs.
Slower calcification means smaller, slower-growing coral reefs, which support about 25% of marine life.
US commercial fish catch in 2007 was worth $3.8 billion, 73% of it from calcifiers and their direct predators.
In the United Kingdom the direct potential loss is put at 14 to 28 percent of shellfish fishery output, about 23 to 88 million pounds.
Arctic fisheries are at risk because acidification harms pteropods and brittle stars at the base of simple Arctic food webs.

definition.text: Ocean alkalinity enhancement is a proposed carbon dioxide removal method that adds alkaline minerals or their products to the ocean surface.

facts.text: Adding alkalinity buffers pH change immediately, which may help organisms where it is added.
Electrochemical methods that strip carbon dioxide from seawater are a related form of alkalinity enhancement.
Such ocean-based methods are still under study, with low technology readiness and many risks.

definition.text: The oceanic carbon cycle is the set of processes that move carbon among pools within the ocean and between the ocean, the atmosphere, Earth's interior and the seafloor.

facts.text: It is central to the global carbon cycle and holds both inorganic and organic carbon.
Three main pumps carry atmospheric carbon dioxide into the ocean interior and spread it through the oceans.
Before the Industrial Revolution the ocean released CO2 to the air; it is now a sink, taking up a net 2.9 billion tonnes of carbon a year on average.
Oceans take up around 25 – 31% of human-emitted CO2.
Cold water dissolves more CO2, so warming seas take up less.
The main net inputs come from the atmosphere and rivers; rivers deliver roughly equal amounts (~0.4 GtC/yr) of dissolved inorganic and organic carbon.
Burial in sediments is the long-term ocean carbon sink and the largest loss from the system; 90% of organic carbon burial happens on deltas, continental shelves and upper slopes.
Dams have cut carbon delivery from rivers to the ocean by an estimated 13% since 1970.

definition.text: Carbon in the ocean is sorted as organic or inorganic, and as dissolved or particulate, giving four pools: DIC, PIC, DOC and POC.

facts.text: Dissolved inorganic carbon is bicarbonate, carbonate and carbon dioxide, including carbonic acid.
Dissolved organic carbon is defined as any organic molecule that passes through a 0.2 μm filter; what the filter catches is particulate organic carbon.
Photosynthesis turns dissolved inorganic carbon into particulate organic carbon; making calcium carbonate turns it into particulate inorganic carbon.

definition.text: The Revelle factor is the ratio of the change in carbon dioxide to the change in dissolved inorganic carbon, showing how readily seawater absorbs more CO2.

facts.text: The lower the Revelle factor, the more carbon dioxide ocean water can take in.
The factor rises as CO2 rises, so the ocean will take up a smaller share of human emissions in future.

title: Iron fertilization

definition.text: Iron fertilization is a geoengineering idea to speed up the ocean's biological pump so it exports more carbon from the surface to the deep sea.

facts.text: The extra export could in theory remove excess carbon dioxide from the air for storage in the deep ocean.
Because the ocean is vast and consumers respond quickly to extra growth, it is hard to tell whether fertilization increases carbon export.
Most of the scientific community does not consider it a reasonable or viable approach.
In about 25 percent of the ocean surface, growth is held back mainly by a lack of iron.

contested_note: Its effectiveness and ecological safety are debated, though researchers note no harm has yet been observed in trials.

definition.text: The permafrost or Arctic carbon cycle is the part of the global carbon cycle that moves carbon between frozen soils, plants and microbes, the atmosphere and back.

facts.text: Permafrost is ground that stays below 0 °C for at least two years in a row.
Permafrost soils cover nearly 9% of Earth's land yet store between 25 and 50% of soil organic carbon.
The northern circumpolar permafrost region holds around 1,460–1,600 Pg of soil organic carbon, more than double the carbon now in the atmosphere.
Radiocarbon dating shows that permafrost carbon is often thousands of years old.
Carbon is locked in as rising ground surfaces from wind- and river-borne sediment and peat are frozen into the permafrost.
Permafrost was a large carbon store often overlooked in early research; attention has grown enormously since the 2000s.

title: Permafrost carbon feedback
article: Permafrost carbon cycle#Carbon release from the permafrost

definition.text: As warming thaws permafrost, long-stored carbon is released as carbon dioxide and methane, adding to the warming that caused the thaw.

facts.text: Permafrost volume in the upper 3 m of ground is expected to fall by about 25% per 1 °C of global warming.
Carbon dioxide from aerobic microbial respiration makes up the overwhelming majority of permafrost emissions.
Thawed ground grows more vegetation, which takes up more carbon and is the main counteracting feedback.
Methane forms in waterlogged, oxygen-free places such as thermokarst lakes left by thawing ice-rich ground.
The IPCC Sixth Assessment Report estimates permafrost releases of 14–175 billion tonnes of CO2 equivalent per 1 °C of warming, against about 40 billion tonnes of annual human CO2 emissions in 2019.
A 2021 assessment estimated that permafrost emissions would raise the social cost of carbon by about 8.4%, though its methods were criticized.
Thawing permafrost is listed among the tipping points in the climate system.

related: Tipping points in the climate system
contested_note: Researchers debate whether rising permafrost emissions mainly come from ancient carbon or from faster respiration of modern plant litter.

definition.text: Subsea permafrost is frozen ground under the seabed of polar continental shelves that were dry land in the last ice age and are now flooded.

facts.text: It covers about 2 million km2 and holds around 560 GtC in organic matter and 45 GtC in methane.
It responds over millennia, so human-driven warming will affect it only hundreds or thousands of years from now.
Under the high-emissions RCP 8.5 scenario, 43 GtC could be released by 2100 and 190 GtC by 2300.

definition.text: Soil carbon is the solid carbon stored in soils, both as organic matter from living things and as carbonate minerals.

facts.text: It supports key soil functions such as holding water, retaining nutrients and building soil structure.
Soils store about 2,700 Gt of carbon, roughly three times the atmosphere's carbon and 240 times annual fossil fuel emissions.
Photosynthesis, respiration and decomposition are the main processes setting how much carbon land stores.
Soil carbon acts as a carbon sink and matters for climate change mitigation and climate models.
Human activities have caused a massive loss of soil organic carbon, but people could also deliberately return carbon to soils.
Warming could change the activity of soil microbes that break down carbon, possibly adding to climate change.

definition.text: Soil organic carbon is the carbon in soil organic matter, the dominant form of soil carbon in humid climates.

facts.text: Soil organic matter is about 50% carbon by dry weight.
Dead plant material, from roots, fallen leaves and crop residue, is its main source; root exudates add more.
Cellulose, starches and proteins break down fast, while lignin, humus and charcoal persist for a long time.
In sandy soils, soil organic carbon raised cation exchange capacity, a measure of fertility.

definition.text: Soil inorganic carbon is carbon held in minerals, from weathered parent rock or from soil minerals reacting with atmospheric CO2.

facts.text: In arid and semi-arid places most soil carbon is in carbonates such as calcite and dolomite.
Carbonates can come from the bedrock or form in the soil itself as pedogenic carbonate.

definition.text: Managing soil carbon means using land in ways that keep or add carbon to soil, since soil-atmosphere carbon exchange is a major part of the global carbon cycle.

facts.text: Humans and farming systems are now the biggest influence on soil carbon variation.
Deforestation, fire, tillage and drainage all cause losses of soil organic carbon.
Drained and tilled peatlands in places such as the Netherlands, East Anglia and Florida have sunk severely as their carbon oxidized.
More soil carbon brings co-benefits: less erosion, higher productivity, cleaner waterways and better water holding.
Agricultural practices that store carbon in soils, called carbon farming, are a land-based carbon dioxide removal method.
Soil carbon offsets can be hard to verify because measurements depend on sampling depth.

title: Soil carbon measurement and reporting
article: Soil carbon#Measuring data on soil organic carbon

definition.text: Under the UN climate convention, countries must estimate and report changes in carbon stocks, including soil carbon, from land use and forestry.

facts.text: The five reported pools are above- and below-ground biomass, dead wood, litter and soil carbon.
Reliable soil carbon estimates are needed for schemes to reduce emissions from deforestation and forest degradation.
A model estimates the topsoil organic carbon stock of EU agricultural soils at 17.63 Gt.

definition.text: Soil erosion is the wearing away of the top layer of soil by water, ice, snow, wind, plants and animals, including people.

facts.text: It can be slow and unnoticed or so fast that it causes a serious loss of topsoil.
On farms it shrinks cropland and production potential, lowers water quality and damages drainage networks.
Unsustainable farming raises erosion one to two orders of magnitude above the natural rate, far faster than soil forms.
About 75 billion tons of soil erode from land each year, about 13–40 times the natural rate.
Water and wind erosion together cause 84% of degraded land, and about 40% of the world's agricultural land is seriously degraded.
Clay-rich and organic-rich soils resist erosion better; plant cover and roots protect soil from both water and wind.
Longer, steeper slopes erode much faster in heavy rain, especially without plant cover.
More intense rainfall expected with climate change will raise erosion unless measures are taken.

definition.text: Rain and the runoff it creates cause four main kinds of soil erosion: splash, sheet, rill and gully erosion.

facts.text: Splash erosion is the first and mildest stage, followed by sheet, then rill, then gully erosion, the most severe.
A raindrop's impact can throw soil particles up to 0.6 m up and 1.5 m sideways on level ground.
Sheet erosion is soil carried by overland flow; rills are small, short-lived channels only a few centimeters deep.
Gully erosion happens when runoff rushes through narrow channels after heavy rain or snowmelt, removing soil to a considerable depth.

definition.text: Wind erosion is the removal of soil by wind, a major force in arid and semi-arid regions.

facts.text: It is a major source of land degradation, desertification, harmful dust and crop damage, especially when raised by deforestation, urbanization and farming.
Wind lifts and carries loose particles (deflation) and wears surfaces down with airborne particles (abrasion).
Dust from wind erosion is a major air pollutant and has been linked to declining coral reef health in the Caribbean and Florida.

definition.text: Tillage erosion is the movement of soil down a field caused by plowing and other tillage.

facts.text: In many fields, especially on hilly land, it is a bigger cause of soil loss than water or wind erosion.
Eroded hilltops are caused by tillage, since water erosion removes soil mainly from mid and lower slopes.
It degrades soil, which can sharply cut crop yields and cause economic losses for farms.

definition.text: Soil eroded mainly from farmland is considered the leading global cause of diffuse water pollution, because of the excess sediment it sends into waterways.

facts.text: Sediment is itself a pollutant and also carries other pollutants such as pesticides and heavy metals.
Silt can smother fish spawning beds by filling the gaps between gravel on stream beds.
Runoff from roads and urban areas carries sediment contaminated with fuel, oil and other chemicals.

title: Universal Soil Loss Equation
article: Soil erosion#Monitoring, measuring and modelling soil erosion

definition.text: The Universal Soil Loss Equation (USLE) is the most widely used model for predicting average yearly soil loss from water erosion on a plot.

facts.text: It multiplies factors for rainfall erosivity, soil erodibility, slope length and steepness, cover and management, and support practices.
It was developed in the 1960s and 1970s and is still the basis of global studies.
It cannot simulate gully erosion, which can make up 10–80% of total erosion on cultivated and grazed land.
All erosion models only roughly match real measured erosion rates.

definition.text: Erosion control is the set of practices that prevent or repair soil erosion, chiefly by keeping land covered with vegetation.

facts.text: Increasing plant cover is the most effective known way to prevent both wind and water erosion.
Terracing is a highly effective method practiced for thousands of years around the world.
Windbreaks of trees and shrubs along fields cut wind erosion and also improve crop microclimates, shelter birds and store carbon.
Mixed cropping, crop rotation and leaving crop residues under conservation tillage all reduce erosion.
Agroforestry, mixing crops with trees, efficiently reduces erosion, especially in rainy tropical climates.
Mangrove roots slow water, trap sediment and bind soils, reducing coastal erosion.
New Deal programs planted 18,000 miles of windbreaks from North Dakota to Texas to fight soil erosion.
Good erosion control manages surface runoff and helps prevent water pollution, soil loss, habitat loss and damage to property.

definition.text: The solubility pump is a physical and chemical process that carries carbon, as dissolved inorganic carbon, from the ocean surface into its depths.

facts.text: It works because CO2 dissolves better in cold water, and deep water forms from cold, dense water at high latitudes.
When deep water rises in warm equatorial seas it releases carbon dioxide back to the air.
About one third of human CO2 emissions, approximately 2 gigatons of carbon per year, are believed to enter the ocean, driven mainly by this pump.
Ocean warming, stronger stratification and slower thermohaline circulation could all weaken it.
Its biological counterpart is the biological pump.
Ocean uptake of CO2 slows climate change but causes ocean acidification.

definition.text: Unlike most gases, carbon dioxide reacts with seawater to form a balance of free CO2, carbonic acid, bicarbonate and carbonate, together called dissolved inorganic carbon.

facts.text: The balance among these forms depends on pH and on seawater's excess of positive ions, called alkalinity.
The greater the alkalinity, the more carbon dioxide seawater can dissolve.
Measuring any two of total inorganic carbon, total alkalinity, pH and pCO2 lets scientists work out the rest.

title: Sulfur cycle

definition.text: The sulfur cycle is the biogeochemical cycle that moves sulfur between rocks, waterways and living things.

facts.text: Sulfur is an essential element of life, found in many proteins, and its compounds can serve in cellular respiration.
The cycle runs through changes in sulfur's oxidation state, from +6 in sulfate to −2 in sulfides.
Its steps include breaking organic sulfur down to hydrogen sulfide, oxidizing sulfide to sulfate, and reducing sulfate back to sulfide.
Microbes that oxidize sulfide often use the energy to fix carbon dioxide.
Earth's main sulfur sink is sulfate in the oceans.
In the sea, sulfate is used to break down buried organic matter and methane; below where sulfate runs out, methane production dominates.
Sulfur takes part in forming fossil fuels and most metal ore deposits.

related: Human impact on the sulfur cycle
distinct_from: Human impact on the sulfur cycle

title: Human impact on the sulfur cycle

definition.text: Burning coal, oil and gas releases sulfur that would otherwise stay locked in rock, greatly increasing sulfur in the air and ocean.

facts.text: Mining coal and extracting petroleum mobilizes 150 × 10^12 gS/yr, more than double the rate of 100 years ago.
Humans barely change the global sulfur pools but massively change the yearly flow of sulfur through the atmosphere.
Sulfur dioxide forms sulfuric acid in the air, causing acid rain; sulfate deposition has risen 30-fold over the most polluted areas.
With acid rain controls cutting sulfur inputs, sulfur deficiency in crops has become widespread in parts of Europe, raising use of sulfur fertilizers.

definition.text: Surface runoff, or overland flow, is water flowing freely over the ground when rain, snowmelt or other water cannot soak into the soil fast enough.

facts.text: It happens when soil is already saturated or rain arrives faster than soil can absorb it, and on roofs and pavement that let no water in.
Runoff is a major part of the water cycle and the main agent of soil erosion by water.
Its main environmental harm is carrying pollutants such as petroleum, herbicides and fertilizers into surface water, groundwater and soil.
More runoff means less groundwater recharge, lowering water tables and worsening droughts for those who rely on wells.
Flooding occurs when a watercourse cannot carry all the runoff flowing downstream.
Remedies include limiting paved surfaces, erosion controls on farms and building sites, green infrastructure, and controls on chemical use.

definition.text: Surface runoff is generated in distinct ways, chiefly when rainfall outpaces infiltration or when rain falls on already saturated soil.

facts.text: Infiltration excess, or Hortonian, overland flow is common in drylands with intense rain and sealed soils, and in paved urban areas.
Saturation excess, or Dunne, runoff occurs when rain keeps falling on soil that is already full of water.
The wetter the soil before a storm, the sooner it saturates and runoff begins.
Water that soaks in upslope can flow sideways through soil and re-emerge near a channel, called subsurface return flow or throughflow.

definition.text: Urban runoff is surface runoff from rain, landscape watering and car washing created by roads, parking lots, roofs and other hard surfaces.

facts.text: Hard surfaces carry polluted stormwater to storm drains instead of letting it soak through soil.
This lowers the water table and causes flooding, since more water stays on the surface.
Most municipal storm sewers discharge untreated stormwater into streams, rivers and bays.
Many towns set building codes, such as narrow sidewalks and pavers set in earth, to let more water soak in.

definition.text: Agricultural runoff is water flowing off farmland that carries chemicals such as nitrates, phosphates, pesticides and herbicides.

facts.text: It happens when chemicals are overused or applied just before heavy rain.
It wastes farm chemicals and threatens downstream ecosystems.
Nitrate fertilizer is especially easily lost in runoff because it is highly soluble and repelled by negatively charged clay.
Concentrated agricultural runoff can cause dead zones in large water bodies.

definition.text: Runoff mitigation combines land use controls, erosion controls, flood control and chemical handling rules to reduce the harm runoff causes.

facts.text: Farmers have used contour farming to protect soil since medieval times.
Construction sites use straw bales, silt fences and scheduling for drier months to slow runoff.
Holding ponds, also called detention basins, buffer peak river flows.
The US Clean Water Act requires urban local governments to run stormwater management programs under discharge permits.

definition.text: An algal bloom is a rapid increase or accumulation in the population of algae in fresh or marine water.

facts.text: Blooms follow nutrients such as nitrogen or phosphorus, from fertilizer runoff or other nutrient pollution, entering the water and causing excessive algal growth.
There is no officially recognized threshold for a bloom; definitions have used chlorophyll above 5-100 ug/L or more than 1000 cells/mL of the blooming species.
Marine blooms rise each spring as storms add nutrients to sunlit water, are tracked by satellite via chlorophyll, and end when nutrients decline and zooplankton graze.
Bloom intensity and occurrence have increased in recent decades, mainly because warming water stimulates growth and lengthens the season; heavy rain can also flush blooms out.
Forecasting, once reliant on water sampling and hydrodynamic models, increasingly combines remote sensing with machine learning.

title: Natural causes of freshwater algal blooms
article: Algal bloom#Freshwater algal blooms > Natural causes of algal blooms

definition.text: Freshwater blooms are not always human-caused: they occur naturally in both eutrophic and oligotrophic lakes.

facts.text: Cyanobacteria are better at nutrient uptake in oligotrophic waters and can fix dissolved atmospheric nitrogen, sustaining large blooms there.
Seasonal overturn in lakes mixes nutrients from deep layers upward, and autumn turnover of stratified lakes can release bio-available phosphorus that triggers blooms.
Phosphorus inputs must be reduced to mitigate blooms containing cyanobacteria.

definition.text: Algal bloom management falls into three categories: mitigation, prevention and control.

facts.text: Mitigation includes routine shellfish toxin monitoring for early warning, restrictions keeping contaminated shellfish off the market, and moving fish pens away from blooms.
Prevention reduces nutrient-laden runoff with more permeable surfaces and vegetation that absorb it before it reaches waterways.

definition.text: A fertilizer is any natural or synthetic material applied to soil or plant tissue to supply plant nutrients.

facts.text: Modern fertilization focuses on the macronutrients nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium (NPK).
Straight fertilizers supply one nutrient; multinutrient or complex fertilizers supply two or more, such as nitrogen and phosphorus together.
