Nitrogen fertilizers are made from ammonia from the energy-intensive Haber-Bosch process, in which natural gas usually supplies the hydrogen.
Phosphate fertilizers come from phosphate rock; billions of kg are mined annually while the size and quality of remaining ore decreases.
Legumes fix atmospheric nitrogen and generally need no nitrogen fertilizer.
About 90% of fertilizers are applied as solids.

definition.text: Synthetic fertilizers used in agriculture have wide-reaching environmental consequences.

facts.text: Only a fraction of nitrogen fertilizer becomes plant matter; the rest accumulates in soil or is lost as runoff, and agricultural runoff is a major contributor to freshwater eutrophication.
Greenhouse gases from manufacture and use of nitrogen fertilizer are about 5% of anthropogenic emissions, one third from production and two thirds from use.
Most synthetic fertilizer depends on fossil fuel, which supplies energy and methane for the hydrogen used in Haber process ammonia.
Phosphate fertilizers can add toxic elements to soil: cadmium in monoammonium phosphate ranged from 0.14 to 50.9 mg/kg, and fluoride from fluorapatite has risen in soils.
Excess fertilizer may break down symbiosis between plant roots and mycorrhizal fungi, while effects on soil animals are still debated.
Overapplication can cause fertilizer burn, damaging or killing the plant.

definition.text: A controlled-release fertilizer is a granulated fertilizer that releases nutrients gradually into the soil.

facts.text: Chemicals that raise nitrogen uptake efficiency let farmers limit polluting nitrogen runoff.
Foliar fertilizers applied to leaves can reduce the total fertilizer used and achieve high efficiency.

definition.text: Governments regulate and subsidize fertilizer to manage its environmental effects.

facts.text: The European Union's Nitrates Directive addresses high nitrate concentrations in runoff, and Britain encourages catchment-sensitive farming.
China has regulated nitrogen fertilizer use and, from 2008, began partly withdrawing fertilizer subsidies for transport, electricity and natural gas.

definition.text: A period in which technology transfer led to a large rise in crop yields, spreading from developed countries and then globally until the late 1980s.

facts.text: The package combined high-yielding cereal varieties, especially dwarf wheat and rice, with chemical fertilizers, pesticides, controlled irrigation and mechanization.
The new seeds need far more fertilizer than traditional varieties; high-yielding varieties absorb more nitrogen, so semi-dwarfing genes were bred in to stop cereals falling over before harvest.
The term was first used by USAID administrator William S. Gaud in a speech on 8 March 1968.
The CGIAR network of agricultural research centres was founded on 19 May 1971, backed by the World Bank, FAO, IFAD and UNDP.
One 2021 estimate says it raised yields by 44% between 1965 and 2010; cereal output more than doubled in developing nations from 1961 to 1985.
Its energy came from fossil fuels: natural gas for fertilizer, oil for pesticides and hydrocarbon-fuelled irrigation.
Efforts to import the model into Africa were generally less successful, owing to corruption, insecurity, weak infrastructure, and scarce irrigation water and varied soils.

title: Green Revolution outcomes and trade-offs
article: Green Revolution#Agricultural production and food security

definition.text: The effects of the Green Revolution on hunger, income, health and the environment are mixed and argued over.

facts.text: A 2012 review found it contributed to widespread poverty reduction, averted hunger for millions and avoided converting thousands of hectares to cultivation.
A 2021 study found it substantially raised income: a ten-year delay would have cost 17% of GDP per capita, and no Green Revolution could have halved developing-world GDP per capita.
A 2020 study of 37 developing countries found modern crop varieties reduced infant mortality by 2.4-5.3 percentage points from a baseline of 18%.

Critics note that more food is not the same as food security, and that the shift brought malnutrition such as iron and vitamin-A deficiencies, with monoculture crops often exported, fed to animals or made into biofuel.
Malthusian critics call it unsustainable, yet a 2021 study found it reduced population growth rather than increasing it.
Effects on wild biodiversity are disputed: higher yields may spare land, but land degradation and nutrient depletion pushed farmers to clear forest to keep production up.
Studies indicate it substantially raised CO2 emissions, while a 2021 study found it cut the land used for agriculture.
Its yield gains have been declining as social and environmental costs become clearer; the Evergreen Revolution aims at 'productivity in perpetuity without associated ecological harm'.

contested_note: Scholars disagree about its net effects on biodiversity, food security and the environment.

definition.text: Methane enters the air from natural and human sources; about 60% of the methane released in 2019 came from human activity.

facts.text: In 2019 about 360 million tons came from human activities and 230 million tons from natural sources; the 2024 total was estimated at 610 million tons, nearly two-thirds human.
The 2021 CCAC and UNEP assessment attributes over 50% of global methane emissions to human activity: fossil fuels 35%, waste 20% and agriculture 40%.
Biogenic methane is made by methanogens, which live in warm, moist soils and in the digestive tracts of ruminants; ruminants emit it by burping and defecating.
Landfills turn anaerobic within about a year of filling, letting methanogens take over; rice paddies emitted about 30 of 400 million metric tons of anthropogenic methane in 2022.
Biomass burning, mostly human-caused, and gas-engine 'methane slip' also release methane.
Converting forest to farmland adds soil nitrogen, which inhibits methane oxidation and weakens soil methanotrophs as sinks.
Methane mixes through the troposphere in about 1-2 years; satellite data show over 80% of emission growth in 2010-2019 was tropical and terrestrial.

definition.text: Capturing and using methane can deliver environmental and economic benefits together.

facts.text: The IEA says about 40% of fossil-fuel methane emissions, 9% of all human methane emissions, could be eliminated at no net cost to firms with existing technology.
The US EPA's 1996 Landfill Rule requires large landfills to collect and combust landfill gas, though it excludes 96% of US landfills.
Satellites such as Sentinel-5P, at about 50 square kilometre resolution, monitor emissions; MethaneSAT aims for 1 kilometre.
